<a id="typ-01"></a>
## TYP-01 - Choose a typeface that fits the context

Match the typeface to the sector and tone: serif for formal sectors, script can be explored for relaxed beauty brands, sans-serif for tech, streaming and messaging.

- **Source:** PDF 72 (printed 71), 73 (printed 72)
- **Applies when:** Selecting brand/product typefaces, especially display type.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Formal sectors (law, accounting, education) suit serif fonts for a classic, polished tone.
- A relaxed, inviting beauty brand could experiment with a script typeface for warmth.
- Tech, music streaming and messaging apps commonly use sans-serif for a sleek, modern feel.

**Mistake:** A typeface whose tone conflicts with the sector.  
**Effect:** Mismatched brand impression.

**Correction:** Pick typefaces whose character matches the audience and sector.  
**Why it works:** Type carries tone before content is read.

**Observable checks:**
- Does the display typeface's character fit the product's sector and audience?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Interpretation (ours, not stated by the PDF):**
- The source frames these as tendencies ('could', 'might'), not rules; readability (TYP-02) still takes priority, especially for body text.

**Related:** [TYP-02](15-typography.md#typ-02), [TYP-03](15-typography.md#typ-03)

<a id="typ-02"></a>
## TYP-02 - Choose readable fonts over decorative ones (and license them)

Fonts must be easy to read as well as attractive; decorative faces hurt readability. Use reliable, properly licensed fonts, with sans-serif for body copy.

- **Source:** PDF 74 (printed 73), 75 (printed 74), 97 (printed 96)
- **Applies when:** Body text, UI text, buttons, and any font decision.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Fonts are about clarity and readability, not only beauty; a poorly chosen font is an Achilles heel.
- The incorrect article card uses blackletter/decorative fonts for the title, body and button; the correct card uses a readable serif title and a clean sans-serif body and button.
- Reliable fonts named by the source: Inter, Gotham, Lato, Open Sans, San Francisco, Helvetica, Manrope, Roboto.
- Ensure fonts are licensed for personal/commercial use; Google Fonts is a reliable free resource.
- Sans-serif fonts for body copy (e.g. Open Sans, Inter, Roboto) are generally more readable than serif fonts such as Times New Roman or Georgia, while fonts can still define the brand.

**Mistake:** Decorative or blackletter faces used for running text and UI controls.  
**Effect:** Hard to read; looks amateurish.

**Correction:** Use a readable sans-serif for body and UI; keep expressive faces (if any) for short display text.  
**Why it works:** Body text is read at length; legibility dominates.

**Observable checks:**
- Is any decorative, script or blackletter font used for paragraphs, labels or buttons?
- Are font licences known for every font in use?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Related:** [TYP-01](15-typography.md#typ-01), [TYP-03](15-typography.md#typ-03)

<a id="typ-03"></a>
## TYP-03 - Use at most two fonts; ideally one with varied weights

More than two font families clutter the UI and look off-brand. Prefer one versatile family using weights and sizes; experienced designers may pair a heading and a body font.

- **Source:** PDF 75 (printed 74), 76 (printed 75), 96 (printed 95), 97 (printed 96)
- **Applies when:** Any interface's type system.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- More than two fonts looks cluttered, confusing and off-brand; the incorrect music app uses four (Poppins, Open Sans, Times, Telex); the correct one uses Inter only.
- Best practice: stick to one versatile font and create variety with weights and sizes.
- Experienced designers can pair two fonts (headings vs paragraphs), e.g. Playfair Display + Source Sans Pro, Raleway + Merriweather, Montserrat + Open Sans; the checklist also cites Playfair Display + Roboto. Resource: figma.com/google-fonts.

**Mistake:** Three or more font families on a screen.  
**Effect:** Messy, inconsistent.

**Correction:** Consolidate to one family (or one heading + one body family).  
**Why it works:** Fewer families give a coherent voice.

**Observable checks:**
- Collect computed font-family values for visible text: more than two distinct families is a violation.

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Interpretation (ours, not stated by the PDF):**
- The incorrect example also uses an all-caps 'DISCOVER MORE' button in a different font; the corrected one uses sentence case. Case is not discussed.

**Source issues / ambiguity:**
- The source writes 'Sources Sans Pro' (presumably Source Sans Pro).

**Related:** [TYP-02](15-typography.md#typ-02), [BAL-03](10-balance.md#bal-03)

<a id="typ-04"></a>
## TYP-04 - Keep body line length to about 45–75 characters (30–40 on mobile)

Body text lines should stay in a comfortable range; full-width paragraphs force long eye travel and cause strain.

- **Source:** PDF 76 (printed 75), 77 (printed 76), 78 (printed 77), 79 (printed 78), 80 (printed 79)
- **Applies when:** Paragraphs and long-form body text.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- The research-backed sweet spot for desktop body copy is 45–75 characters per line; for mobile, 30–40.
- Breaking the range can overwhelm readers or make them lose their place, but these are guidelines, not strict rules; adjust for content, layout and device.
- Measure with tools such as a Figma 'Character counter' plugin or online counters.
- The incorrect design stretches body text across the whole page width; one correct design centres a text block limited to 75 characters per line under the hero; another left-aligns the text with line length under 75 characters.

**Mistake:** Paragraphs spanning the full page or container width (well over 75 characters).  
**Effect:** Eyes travel far from line end to next line start; eye strain and lower readability.

**Correction:** Constrain the text measure (e.g. max-width around 60–75ch for desktop body text).  
**Why it works:** Shorter measures make line returns easy.

**Observable checks:**
- Estimate characters per line at common desktop widths: is it above about 75?
- In CSS: does the paragraph container have a max-width (e.g. in ch)?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- Guidelines, not strict rules: device- and content-specific adjustments are allowed.

**Source issues / ambiguity:**
- In the first correct design the text block is centred on the page but its lines are left-aligned (ragged right); 'center-aligned' refers to block placement, not text-align:center.

**Related:** [ALN-03](05-alignment.md#aln-03), [WS-04](08-whitespace.md#ws-04)

<a id="typ-05"></a>
## TYP-05 - Break up long paragraphs and space them

Split long blocks into short paragraphs with space between them to create natural stopping points.

- **Source:** PDF 81 (printed 80), 97 (printed 96)
- **Applies when:** Content-heavy sections and descriptions.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Long blocks overwhelm; splitting a long paragraph into shorter ones gives a visual break, eases scanning and creates natural stopping points.
- Leave adequate space between paragraphs in longer text blocks.

**Mistake:** One long paragraph in a card or section.  
**Effect:** Readers are overwhelmed and skim past.

**Correction:** Split into two to four short paragraphs with paragraph spacing.  
**Why it works:** Visual chunks are easier to digest.

**Observable checks:**
- Is there any paragraph longer than roughly 5–6 lines at its rendered width?
- Is there visible spacing between paragraphs?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Related:** [IC-04](16-interaction-cost.md#ic-04), [TYP-06](15-typography.md#typ-06)

<a id="typ-06"></a>
## TYP-06 - Use descriptive subheadings

Subheadings act as a roadmap: they make content scannable and give a preview; icons, lines or extra space can make them stand out.

- **Source:** PDF 82 (printed 81)
- **Applies when:** Long text sections, product descriptions, articles.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Subheadings grab attention, give a sneak peek and make content scannable and digestible; icons, lines and extra space help them stand out.
- The corrected example uses a descriptive title plus three subheadings with emoji icons separated by thin dividers.

**Mistake:** A generic title over one undivided paragraph.  
**Effect:** No structure to scan.

**Correction:** Descriptive title plus subheadings per topic.  
**Why it works:** Readers can jump to what interests them.

**Observable checks:**
- Does long content have subheadings that describe each section's content?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Related:** [TYP-05](15-typography.md#typ-05), [IC-04](16-interaction-cost.md#ic-04)

<a id="typ-07"></a>
## TYP-07 - Avoid pure black/white text; make headings darker than body

Use off-black or dark grey for headings and a lighter grey for body text (and the light-on-dark equivalents) instead of pure #000/#FFF for everything.

- **Source:** PDF 83 (printed 82), 96 (printed 95), 97 (printed 96)
- **Applies when:** Text colour tokens in light and dark themes.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Avoid pure black #000000 text on white and pure white #FFFFFF text on dark backgrounds, for readability and visual harmony.
- Correct values shown: dark theme heading #F2F2F2 and body #CACACA; light theme heading #1A1A1A and body #4E4E4E. Incorrect: #FFFFFF/#FFFFFF and #000000/#000000.
- Checklist: use darker colours for headings and lighter for paragraphs; avoid pure black/white for both headings and paragraphs, and avoid the same colour for both.

**Mistake:** Headings and body in the same pure black (or pure white).  
**Effect:** Harsh and flat; no colour hierarchy between heading and body.

**Correction:** Off-black heading with a softer grey body (or off-white heading with light-grey body on dark).  
**Why it works:** Softer contrast is soothing while the step between heading and body adds hierarchy.

**Observable checks:**
- Are text colours exactly #000000 or #FFFFFF?
- Do heading and body share the same colour?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Interpretation (ours, not stated by the PDF):**
- Body greys must still pass contrast (TYP-09); 'lighter' is not 'too light'.

**Source issues / ambiguity:**
- The correct dark card still uses a pure black background; the rule concerns text colours.

**Related:** [VH-04](02-visual-hierarchy.md#vh-04), [TYP-09](15-typography.md#typ-09)

<a id="typ-08"></a>
## TYP-08 - Use heavier weights for headings, regular for body

Headings in bold, semibold or medium; paragraphs in regular (sometimes light) so they don't compete. Light headings can work only when size and colour carry the hierarchy.

- **Source:** PDF 84 (printed 83), 85 (printed 84), 96 (printed 95), 97 (printed 96)
- **Applies when:** Type scale definitions.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Go thicker for headings (bold, semibold, medium) and thinner for paragraphs (regular, sometimes light) so text doesn't compete; incorrect: heading Regular with body Regular; correct: heading Bold with body Regular.
- Exception: sites such as Pleo and Linear use lighter heading weights; this works because they use colour (darker headings, lighter paragraphs) and above all size (headings much bigger).

**Mistake:** Heading and body in the same weight (and similar size).  
**Effect:** Weak hierarchy.

**Correction:** Increase heading weight, or keep it light but make it much larger and darker.  
**Why it works:** Weight or size difference marks the heading.

**Observable checks:**
- Do heading and body share the same font-weight? If so, is the heading substantially larger and darker?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- Light-weight headings are acceptable when size and colour clearly establish hierarchy.

**Related:** [TYP-11](15-typography.md#typ-11), [TYP-10](15-typography.md#typ-10)

<a id="typ-09"></a>
## TYP-09 - Text must have sufficient contrast (at least WCAG AA)

Don't trade readability for minimalism: avoid very light grey text and faint-on-faint colour pairs; for most text aim for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1.

- **Source:** PDF 86 (printed 85), 93 (printed 92), 95 (printed 94), 97 (printed 96)
- **Applies when:** All text, including body copy on coloured cards and button labels.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Avoid too-light colours: very light grey text causes squinting, especially for people with poorer vision; minimal does not mean readable.
- Incorrect body text #A9A9A9 on white is labelled WCAG AA fail / AAA fail; correct #626262 is labelled AA pass / AAA pass.
- Faint text on a faint background (e.g. white on light purple) fails; dark text on the same purple passes. For most text a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 is considered accessible.
- Tools: WebAIM, Coolors.co, the Figma Contrast plugin by WillowTree. Checklist: meet at least WCAG Level AA; don't accept bad contrast for aesthetics.

**Mistake:** Light grey body text, or white text on pastel/light colour backgrounds (including button labels).  
**Effect:** Hard or impossible to read for many users; accessibility failure.

**Correction:** Darken text (or background) until the ratio is at least 4.5:1 for normal text; verify with a contrast checker.  
**Why it works:** Contrast is the precondition for legibility.

**Observable checks:**
- Compute the contrast ratio for each text/background pair; flag below 4.5:1 for normal-size text.
- Check text on buttons, chips and coloured cards, not only on the page background.

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Source issues / ambiguity:**
- SUPPLEMENTAL CHECK (not from the PDF): by the WCAG formula #626262 on white is about 6.1:1, which passes AA (4.5:1) but not AAA for normal text (7:1). The source's 'AAA pass' label appears to be inaccurate; verify AAA claims with a checker.

**Related:** [CON-01](06-contrast.md#con-01), [TYP-07](15-typography.md#typ-07), [DEP-09](13-depth.md#dep-09)

<a id="typ-10"></a>
## TYP-10 - Avoid extra-light and thin weights for body text

Very thin strokes blend into the background or break apart on small screens and in poor lighting; use regular or medium for bulk text.

- **Source:** PDF 87 (printed 86), 96 (printed 95)
- **Applies when:** Body and UI text.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Extra-light weights look elegant but thin strokes blend or break apart on small screens or in bad lighting, harming older adults and people with visual impairments.
- Stick to regular or medium for bulk text; the checklist names Inter Extra Light / Inter Thin as weights to avoid.

**Mistake:** Paragraphs set in Extra-light (200) or Thin (100).  
**Effect:** Hard to read.

**Correction:** Use Regular (400) or Medium (500) for body text.  
**Why it works:** Stroke thickness drives legibility at small sizes.

**Observable checks:**
- Is any body/UI text set below font-weight 400 (especially 100–300)?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Related:** [TYP-08](15-typography.md#typ-08), [TYP-09](15-typography.md#typ-09)

<a id="typ-11"></a>
## TYP-11 - Use size to communicate importance

Size is the most direct way to establish hierarchy: make the most important text clearly the largest.

- **Source:** PDF 88 (printed 87), 89 (printed 88)
- **Applies when:** Headlines vs supporting text, warnings vs instructions.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Size is the most direct way to establish hierarchy; bigger attracts more attention.
- Traffic-light card: making 'Start the engine and go full speed' large and 'Wait until you see the green light!' tiny could lead users to act too soon; the correct version enlarges the warning.
- Watch card: a heading much bigger than the body creates clear hierarchy even with the same colours and fonts; a title the same size as the body text doesn't grab attention.

**Mistake:** Critical text small while secondary text is large, or a title the same size as body text.  
**Effect:** Users read the wrong thing first or miss the title.

**Correction:** Scale type by importance; the key message or title gets the largest size.  
**Why it works:** Size is read before content.

**Observable checks:**
- Is the most important sentence the largest text in its group?
- Is the title noticeably larger than body text?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Source issues / ambiguity:**
- On the watch-card page the correct example is shown first (top) and the incorrect second (bottom).

**Related:** [VH-03](02-visual-hierarchy.md#vh-03), [TYP-08](15-typography.md#typ-08)

<a id="typ-12"></a>
## TYP-12 - Use readable font sizes (16px body baseline)

Main text is usually 16px; avoid main text below 12px. It depends on platform and font, so test on devices.

- **Source:** PDF 90 (printed 89), 96 (printed 95), 97 (printed 96)
- **Applies when:** Body text and UI labels.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Incorrect card: title 32px, tabs 16px, body 10px. Correct: 32px, 16px, body 16px.
- The gold standard for main text is usually 16px, though not one-size-fits-all (platform, font).
- Avoid main text below 12px: hard to read, users bounce, accessibility issues. Test on different devices and ask others.
- Checklist: avoid font sizes smaller than 10px (platform dependent).

**Mistake:** Body copy at 10–11px.  
**Effect:** Unreadable for many; accessibility issues.

**Correction:** Set body to around 16px and keep main text at or above 12px.  
**Why it works:** Readability is the main goal of text.

**Observable checks:**
- Flag any main/body text below 12px and any text below 10px; compare body size with 16px.

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- Platform and font specifics may justify deviations; test on target devices.

**Source issues / ambiguity:**
- Two thresholds appear: avoid main text below 12px (pdf p90) and avoid any font smaller than 10px (checklist, pdf p96). Treat <12px main text as a problem and <10px as a strong violation.

**Related:** [TYP-13](15-typography.md#typ-13), [TYP-09](15-typography.md#typ-09)

<a id="typ-13"></a>
## TYP-13 - Give body text generous line-height (about 1.5–1.6×)

With the same font, size and colour, increasing body line-height alone improves readability; for about 16px text aim for 150–160%.

- **Source:** PDF 91 (printed 90)
- **Applies when:** Paragraph text.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Bigger line-height is a 'secret weapon': the two paragraphs differ only in line height.
- For about 16px text aim for 1.5–1.6× (150–160%); above 2× text looks like it floats; below 1.2× looks cramped.

**Mistake:** Tight leading (about 1.1–1.2) on paragraphs.  
**Effect:** Cramped, harder to read.

**Correction:** line-height 1.5–1.6 for body text.  
**Why it works:** Space between lines guides the eye to the next line.

**Observable checks:**
- Compute line-height/font-size for paragraphs: flag below 1.2 (cramped) or above 2.0 (floating); target 1.5–1.6 around 16px.

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Related:** [TYP-14](15-typography.md#typ-14), [TYP-12](15-typography.md#typ-12)

<a id="typ-14"></a>
## TYP-14 - Use tighter line-height for headings than for paragraphs

Headings look compact and impactful with smaller line-height; paragraphs need larger line-height. The bigger the text, the smaller the line-height ratio.

- **Source:** PDF 92 (printed 91), 95 (printed 94), 96 (printed 95), 97 (printed 96)
- **Applies when:** Type scale definitions.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Use a smaller line-height for headings (compact, impactful) and a larger one for paragraphs (inviting, easier to read); example values: heading 120%, paragraph 160%.
- Rule: bigger text gets a smaller line-height, smaller text a bigger one; e.g. a 36px heading at about 1.3× (130%).
- Checklist: avoid a bigger line-height for headings than paragraphs.

**Mistake:** Loose heading leading with tight paragraph leading (the inverse).  
**Effect:** The heading falls apart visually and body text is cramped.

**Correction:** Headings about 1.1–1.3; body about 1.5–1.6.  
**Why it works:** Large text already has visual space between lines; small text needs more.

**Observable checks:**
- Is heading line-height ratio lower than paragraph line-height ratio?
- Flag headings with line-height ≥ 1.5 when body text is ≤ 1.3.

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Source issues / ambiguity:**
- Visual ambiguity: in the incorrect card, the annotation labels read 'Line-height: 120%' and '160%' (the same as the correct card), but the rendering clearly shows a loose heading and tight paragraph. The labels appear to describe the target values, not the incorrect card. This knowledge base follows the rendered visual and the text.

**Related:** [TYP-13](15-typography.md#typ-13)
